---
title: "Life Expectancy and National Income: A Cross-Sectional and Time-Series Correlation Analysis"
subtitle: "Reported following the STROBE framework for observational studies"
---

<span class="kicker">Machine Learning for Social Science &nbsp;·&nbsp; Boston, MA</span>

::: {.lead}
This post treats a familiar relationship &mdash; life expectancy and income &mdash;
as a small observational study, reported in the structure epidemiologists use
for cross-sectional and cohort research (the STROBE guidelines). The aim is not
the epidemiology; it is to use a rigorous reporting frame to ask a question this
whole series has been circling: does a correlation observed **across units at one
point in time** describe the same relationship as a correlation observed
**within one unit over time**?
:::

## Abstract

**Design.** Observational, correlational study combining a cross-sectional
comparison across countries with a longitudinal time series within a single
country. **Objective.** To estimate the Pearson correlation between life
expectancy and GDP per capita (i) across 175 countries at one point in time
(2023&ndash;2024) and (ii) within the United States annually from 1960 to 2024,
and to compare the two. **Methods.** Publicly available national statistics;
Pearson correlation coefficients computed on both untransformed and
log-transformed income. **Results.** Both designs show a strong positive
association: r = 0.86 (log income) in the cross-section (n = 175, p &lt; 10<sup>&minus;50</sup>)
and r = 0.97 (log income) in the US time series (n = 65, p &lt; 10<sup>&minus;39</sup>).
**Conclusion.** The correlation is strong and positive under both designs, but a
correlation coefficient alone cannot distinguish a direct effect of income from
a shared trend or common cause &mdash; a limitation addressed further in the
discussion.

## Introduction

### Background and rationale

The association between national income and population health is one of the
best-documented empirical regularities in economic demography, generally
credited to Samuel Preston's 1975 cross-national comparison of life expectancy
and GDP per capita (the "Preston curve"). The relationship is concave: a given
increase in income buys much more life expectancy in a poor country than in a
rich one. It is also, definitionally, a **cross-sectional** finding &mdash;
different countries compared at a single point in time.

A separate and logically independent question is whether the same association
holds **within** a country as it develops over time. This distinction matters
because a relationship that is real and strong in a cross-section need not
describe what happens to any single unit as it moves through time &mdash; a
problem long recognized in the social sciences as the ecological fallacy
(Robinson, 1950) and, in this specific empirical setting, documented directly by
Preston himself: national time series of income growth explain only a modest
share of a country's own gains in life expectancy over the twentieth century,
with the cross-sectional curve itself shifting upward decade by decade. This
series has now checked that same cross-section/time-series distinction for
three different pairs of variables (women's labor force participation and
income; urbanization and income; and here, life expectancy and income), because
it is a general methodological question, not one specific to any variable pair.

### Objectives

1. To estimate the Pearson correlation between life expectancy and GDP per
   capita across countries at one point in time (a cross-sectional design).
2. To estimate the Pearson correlation between the same two variables within a
   single country (the United States) across a 65-year period (a time-series
   design).
3. To compare the two estimates and consider what a simple correlation
   coefficient can, and cannot, establish about the relationship in each design.

## Methods

### Study design

Two designs are reported side by side: (i) a cross-sectional design, in which
each country contributes a single observation at approximately the same point
in time; and (ii) a time-series design, in which a single country (the United
States) contributes one observation per year over 65 consecutive years. No
intervention, treatment assignment, or manipulation of any kind was involved in
either design; both are purely observational.

### Setting

The cross-sectional design covers all countries for which both variables were
available in the sources described below, observed in the most recent year
each source publishes (GDP per capita: 2023; life expectancy: most recent
CIA World Factbook estimate, referenced 2024). The time-series design covers
the United States, annually, from 1960 (the first year both source series
report) to 2024.

### Participants (units of analysis)

**Cross-section:** All sovereign states and territories for which a numeric
value was available for both life expectancy and GDP per capita in the sources
below, matched by country name (with manual reconciliation of naming
differences, e.g., "South Korea" vs. "Korea, Rep."). Of 229 countries and
territories with a life expectancy figure, 175 (76%) had a matching GDP per
capita figure and were included; the remainder lacked a GDP estimate in the
source used (chiefly small territories and countries without recent World Bank
national accounts data, e.g., North Korea, Cuba, Eritrea) and were excluded.

**Time series:** All calendar years 1960&ndash;2024 for the United States for
which both series report a value. No years were missing; n = 65.

### Variables

**Outcome (both designs):** Life expectancy at birth, in years &mdash; the
average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates
at the time of observation stayed constant over its lifetime.

**Exposure (both designs):** GDP per capita &mdash; gross domestic product
divided by population. Cross-sectional GDP per capita is expressed in current
US dollars; time-series GDP per capita is expressed in constant 2010 US
dollars (to remove the effect of US inflation over the 65-year window, which a
current-dollar figure would otherwise confound with real income growth).

### Data sources and measurement

| Design | Variable | Source | URL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cross-section | Life expectancy, ~2024 | CIA World Factbook, via Bamwor World Encyclopedia | <https://bamwor.com/en/countries-by-life-expectancy> |
| Cross-section | GDP per capita, 2023 | World Bank Open Data, via Lumistats | <https://lumistats.com/rankings/gdp/> |
| Time series | Life expectancy, 1960&ndash;2024 (US) | World Bank World Development Indicators, series SPDYNLE00INUSA, via FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) | <https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/SPDYNLE00INUSA> |
| Time series | GDP per capita, 1960&ndash;2024 (US), constant 2010 US$ | World Bank World Development Indicators, series NYGDPPCAPKDUSA, via FRED | <https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/NYGDPPCAPKDUSA> |

### Bias

Three sources of potential bias are noted. First, the cross-section combines
life expectancy from one producer (CIA World Factbook) and GDP per capita from
another (World Bank), reported in different years (~2024 and 2023
respectively) and compiled by different aggregator sites; this is a
comparability concern rather than a random-error concern, since it could shift
the estimated correlation in either direction depending on how each source's
methodology and reference year diverge. Second, both cross-sectional
variables, and both time-series variables, come from a single World Bank
lineage in the time-series case, reducing (but not eliminating) that specific
concern for the within-country design. Third, and most importantly for
interpretation: no adjustment was made, in either design, for variables that
plausibly affect both life expectancy and income at once (education, disease
environment, war, and &mdash; specific to the time-series design &mdash; the
passage of calendar time itself, during which medical technology improved
independently of any single country's income growth). This is addressed
further under Limitations.

### Study size

Study size was determined by data availability rather than by a power
calculation: all countries with matched data in the cross-section (n = 175),
and all years with matched data in the US time series (n = 65).

### Quantitative variables

GDP per capita was analyzed in two forms in both designs: untransformed
(dollars) and natural-log-transformed. The log transform was included because
the Preston curve is a well-documented **concave** relationship &mdash; equal
dollar increases in income are associated with larger life-expectancy gains at
low income than at high income &mdash; and a linear (Pearson) correlation on
untransformed income will understate the strength of a genuinely monotonic but
curved association. Life expectancy was analyzed untransformed (years) in both
designs.

### Statistical methods

All associations are reported as the Pearson product-moment correlation
coefficient, computed the same way in both designs &mdash; the only difference
is what the index runs over:

**Cross-section** (country *i* = 1...*n*):

r = &Sigma;<sub>i</sub>(x<sub>i</sub> &minus; x&#772;)(y<sub>i</sub> &minus; y&#772;) / &radic;[&Sigma;<sub>i</sub>(x<sub>i</sub> &minus; x&#772;)&sup2; &middot; &Sigma;<sub>i</sub>(y<sub>i</sub> &minus; y&#772;)&sup2;]

**Time series** (year *t* = 1...*T*, single country):

r = &Sigma;<sub>t</sub>(x<sub>t</sub> &minus; x&#772;)(y<sub>t</sub> &minus; y&#772;) / &radic;[&Sigma;<sub>t</sub>(x<sub>t</sub> &minus; x&#772;)&sup2; &middot; &Sigma;<sub>t</sub>(y<sub>t</sub> &minus; y&#772;)&sup2;]

No regression model was fit in either design; only the correlation coefficient,
its two-sided p-value (against the null of r = 0), and sample size are
reported. This choice is deliberate and is returned to in the Discussion.

**Why a correlation coefficient is a valid tool here, and where it stops being
one.** A Pearson correlation is a valid summary of the strength and direction
of a *linear* (or, after transformation, monotonic) association between two
variables, and its significance test is valid whenever observations are
independent and the usual regularity conditions hold. It becomes an
**unreliable guide to the underlying relationship** in at least three
situations relevant here. First, when the association is driven by a **third
variable** that independently moves both x and y &mdash; classically, a
confounder. Second, when the data are **aggregated units** rather than the
individual-level units the relationship is really about (the ecological
fallacy): a correlation between country-level averages can differ in sign or
magnitude from the correlation that would be observed within any single
country, and vice versa. Third, in time series specifically, when both
variables share a **common trend** &mdash; two unrelated series that both rise
steadily over decades will correlate strongly even absent any causal link
between them, because "time" itself is the omitted third variable. All three
concerns are directly relevant to interpreting the results below, and are
addressed in the Discussion.

**Why life expectancy and GDP per capita are a good pair for illustrating
this.** The relationship is real, large, well-replicated, and has a plausible
direct mechanism (income buys nutrition, sanitation, and medical care) &mdash;
so it is not a spurious or trivial example. But it is simultaneously a textbook
case for every one of the three correlation pitfalls above: countries differ on
many confounders correlated with income (education, governance, disease
burden); the cross-sectional relationship is explicitly known, from Preston's
own work, to have shifted over historical time in a way that a single
correlation coefficient cannot reveal; and the US time series in particular
spans a period (1960&ndash;2024) of dramatic medical progress that plausibly
drove much of the life-expectancy gain independent of income growth. It is,
in other words, a relationship where "the correlation is strong" is true and
also nowhere near the end of the story.

## Results

### Participants

175 of 229 countries and territories with a life expectancy estimate (76%)
had a matching GDP per capita estimate and were included in the cross-section.
All 65 years from 1960 to 2024 were included in the US time series (100% of
the available window).

### Descriptive statistics

<div style="overflow-x:auto;">
| Design | Variable | n | Mean | Median | SD | Min | Max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cross-section (countries, 2023&ndash;24) | Life expectancy (years) | 175 | 74.4 | 75.6 | 7.0 | 54.4 | 89.8 |
| Cross-section (countries, 2023&ndash;24) | GDP per capita (current US$) | 175 | 20,883 | 7,133 | 33,282 | 251 | 256,800 |
| Time series (US, 1960&ndash;2024) | Life expectancy (years) | 65 | 75.0 | 75.4 | 3.0 | 69.8 | 78.9 |
| Time series (US, 1960&ndash;2024) | GDP per capita (constant 2010 US$) | 65 | 40,950 | 39,448 | 13,780 | 18,992 | 66,857 |
</div>

The cross-sectional GDP per capita distribution is heavily right-skewed (mean
more than 2.9 times the median), consistent with the well-known long right
tail of the global income distribution; the US time-series GDP per capita is
comparatively symmetric (mean close to median) over its narrower 3.5-fold
range.

### The data

**Cross-section**, 175 countries, GDP per capita (log scale) vs. life
expectancy:

<canvas id="crossPlot"></canvas>
</div>

**Time series**, United States, 1960&ndash;2024, one point per year:

### Main results

<div style="overflow-x:auto;">
| Design | GDP form | r | p | n |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cross-section (countries) | Untransformed | 0.62 | &lt; 10<sup>&minus;19</sup> | 175 |
| Cross-section (countries) | Log-transformed | **0.86** | &lt; 10<sup>&minus;52</sup> | 175 |
| Time series (US, 1960&ndash;2024) | Untransformed | 0.95 | &lt; 10<sup>&minus;31</sup> | 65 |
| Time series (US, 1960&ndash;2024) | Log-transformed | **0.97** | &lt; 10<sup>&minus;39</sup> | 65 |
</div>

In both designs, the log-transformed correlation is stronger than the
untransformed one, consistent with the expected concave (diminishing-returns)
shape of the relationship. No other analyses (subgroup, sensitivity, or
adjusted) were conducted; only the unadjusted correlation coefficients
specified in advance are reported.

## Discussion

### Key results

Both the cross-sectional and the time-series design show a strong, positive,
statistically significant correlation between life expectancy and GDP per
capita, and in both designs the relationship strengthens under a log
transform of income. Taken at face value, the two designs agree: countries
with higher income tend to have higher life expectancy, and the United States'
own life expectancy has risen closely alongside its own income over 65 years.

### Limitations

This is a correlational analysis of unadjusted, aggregated national statistics,
and its limitations follow directly from the three concerns raised in Methods.
No confounders were controlled for, so neither r cannot separate a direct
income&rarr;health effect from confounding by education, governance, disease
environment, or (in the time series) simple calendar time, during which
antibiotics, vaccination, and neonatal care advanced independent of any single
country's income growth. The cross-section mixes two data producers observed
in different years, a comparability limitation noted above. And a single
Pearson r, by construction, reports only the strength of the association at
the level analyzed &mdash; it says nothing about whether the *same*
relationship (the same slope, the same curve) holds across the two designs,
only that a relationship of some strength holds in each. A companion piece in
this series (the "Preston curve" post on the Goldin data pattern) shows
directly, by plotting the US time path against the cross-sectional curve, that
the two need not coincide even when both correlations are strong.

### Interpretation

A cautious reading of these results is that income and life expectancy move
together, strongly, both across countries and within the United States over
time &mdash; but a correlation coefficient alone cannot say whether income is
doing the causal work, in either design, or how much of each estimate reflects
a genuine income effect versus a shared trend or common cause. The very high
time-series correlation (r = 0.97 on log income) is exactly the pattern one
would also expect to see if life expectancy and income were both simply rising
over the same 65 years for largely unrelated reasons (medical technology
improving on its own trajectory; income growing on its own) &mdash; the
correlation coefficient, by design, cannot distinguish these two stories from
each other.

### Generalizability

The cross-sectional estimate describes the relationship across the specific
set of 175 countries included here at one point in time and should not be
assumed to describe the relationship *within* any individual country as it
develops; the time-series estimate describes the United States specifically
and should not be assumed to generalize to other countries, which may follow a
different path (as this series has already shown directly for female labor
force participation, where three of four countries with long-run data showed
no U-shape at all despite a robust cross-sectional U).

## Conclusion and next steps

Both designs here return a strong, statistically significant, unadjusted
correlation between income and life expectancy, and the log-income version is
stronger than the linear one in each case &mdash; a first, purely descriptive
answer to whether "the correlation holds" across designs. What an unadjusted
correlation coefficient cannot deliver is a quantified relationship one could
use to predict, compare magnitudes across the two designs on a common scale,
or begin separating a shared time trend from a direct association. The next
post in this series will fit an unadjusted ordinary least squares (OLS)
regression to both the cross-sectional and time-series data, which will add:
an explicit slope (years of life expectancy per log-dollar of income) directly
comparable between the two designs; an R&sup2; describing how much of the
variance in life expectancy each design's income measure accounts for; and
residual plots that can start to reveal *where* the two designs' relationships
diverge, rather than only *whether* a correlation exists in each. That step
remains, deliberately, still unadjusted for confounders &mdash; a fully
adjusted model is a further step beyond it.
